- If sentiment is consistently positive or neutral over recent days, model tends to underpredict upward moves; increase forecast slightly above historical mean.
- If sentiment is negative or shows recent decline, model often overpredicts downward moves; reduce forecast slope or add buffer below observed trend.
- When model shows steady, small upward drift (e.g., +0.05–0.10 per day) but true outcome spikes sharply, model is lagging; adjust forecast to anticipate early breakout.
- If model forecast is flat or slowly rising while true outcome shows strong mean reversion, reduce forecast slope and add downward bias to reflect volatility correction.
- In cases where sentiment is neutral or mixed, model often overestimates volatility; cap forecast range to avoid extreme outliers.
- If model forecast is consistently above true outcome with no clear trend, consider mean reversion bias — reduce forecast by 1–2% of recent average deviation.
- For short-term (1–3 day) forecasts, avoid linear extrapolation; use sentiment-weighted smoothing to capture sudden sentiment-driven shifts.
- If sentiment history shows recent spikes (e.g., >0.7) followed by model overprediction, apply “overshoot correction” — reduce forecast by 0.5–1.5% per day after spike.
